flashcards.q: What two dunder methods define the iterator protocol?
flashcards.a: __iter__ (returns an iterator, usually self) and __next__ (returns the next value or raises StopIteration).

flashcards.q: Is every iterator a generator? Is every generator an iterator?
flashcards.a: Every generator is an iterator. Not every iterator is a generator — a hand-written class with __iter__/__next__, a zip object, or a file object are iterators but not generators.

flashcards.q: Approx memory: list(range(10_000_000)) of ints vs a generator over the same range.
flashcards.a: List: ~350-400MB (pointer array + boxed int objects, each int >=28 bytes). Generator: ~200 bytes, constant regardless of N.

flashcards.q: What happens when you call a function containing `yield`?
flashcards.a: No code in the function runs. It immediately returns a generator object; the body only executes on next()/iteration.

flashcards.q: What happens if you iterate an already-exhausted generator a second time?
flashcards.a: It raises StopIteration immediately, which a for-loop or list() interprets as zero items. No error or warning is raised — this is a silent bug source.

flashcards.q: What does `yield from sub_gen()` preserve that a manual `for x in sub_gen(): yield x` does not?
flashcards.a: It forwards send()/throw()/close() calls into the sub-generator, and captures the sub-generator's return value as the yield-from expression's result.

flashcards.q: What must you do before calling gen.send(value) with a non-None value, and why?
flashcards.a: Prime the generator first with next(gen) (or gen.send(None)). Otherwise TypeError, because there's no suspended yield expression yet to receive the sent value.
Raises GeneratorExit at the generator's current suspend point, running any finally/with cleanup code. CPython calls this automatically on garbage collection.

flashcards.q: Since Python 3.7 (PEP 479), what happens if a StopIteration leaks out of a generator's body unhandled?
flashcards.a: It is converted into a RuntimeError instead of silently truncating the enclosing for-loop.

flashcards.q: Does itertools.groupby group all items sharing a key, like SQL GROUP BY?
flashcards.a: No. It groups only consecutive runs of equal keys, like Unix uniq. Input must be pre-sorted by the key or it silently produces many small groups.

flashcards.q: What is the worst-case memory cost of itertools.tee(it, 2)?
flashcards.a: If one branch runs far ahead of the other, tee buffers every element the slow branch hasn't consumed yet, approaching the cost of materializing the whole sequence as a list.

flashcards.q: Name three cases where a generator is the wrong tool.
flashcards.a: You need len() up front; you need random access/indexing or multiple passes; the dataset is small enough that materializing is free and the generator only costs debuggability.
No. sorted() must consume the entire input before producing the first output, so it fully materializes internally regardless of the input type.

flashcards.q: What does itertools.islice(gen, 100, 110) do, and what can't it do?
flashcards.a: Skips the first 100 items then yields the next 10, forward-only. It cannot seek backward or index like a list slice can.
